title: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion
subtitle: Frontal or parieto-occipital catheter, valve and peritoneal catheter

indications: Symptomatic hydrocephalus that needs permanent CSF diversion: post-haemorrhagic, post-infective (once the CSF is sterile), congenital, tumour-related when the obstruction will persist, and normal pressure hydrocephalus selected after assessment.
Conversion of an external ventricular drain that cannot be weaned.
Obstructive hydrocephalus in which endoscopic third ventriculostomy is unsuitable or has failed.
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension with failing vision, in selected patients and after neuro-ophthalmology input.
contraindications: Active CSF infection, or untreated infection elsewhere (skin, urine, chest, peritoneum): treat first and shunt when the CSF is sterile.
Hostile peritoneum: active peritonitis, recent abdominal surgery with contamination, or extensive adhesions. Choose another distal site.
CSF with very high protein or fresh blood, which blocks valves: drain externally until it clears.
Obstructive hydrocephalus suitable for endoscopic third ventriculostomy, which avoids a lifelong implant.
Skin over the planned course that is thin, broken or infected, especially in a premature infant.
preparation: Confirm the indication on recent imaging, the ventricle size, and the planned entry point and side. Small ventricles favour navigation or ultrasound guidance.
CSF results (cell count, protein, culture) if a drain is present or infection is possible.

Choose the valve with the consultant: fixed-pressure or programmable, with or without an anti-siphon or gravitational device, considering age, mobility and the cause of the hydrocephalus. Check that the programmable valve is compatible with future MRI.
Book the patient first on the list where possible and minimise theatre traffic: shunt infection rates are lower with a standardised protocol.

Consent should include shunt infection, shunt blockage or disconnection needing revision (the commonest long-term problem), over-drainage with headaches or subdural collections, under-drainage, intracerebral haemorrhage or seizures from the ventricular catheter, abdominal complications (bowel injury, pseudocyst, hernia), and the likelihood of further shunt surgery during life.
positioning: Supine with the head on a horseshoe or ring, turned away from the operative side.
A shoulder roll so that the head, neck, chest and abdomen form a straight line for the tunnel.
Keep the abdomen accessible; in infants, attend to warming throughout.
equipment: Ventricular catheter, valve and distal catheter, preferably antibiotic-impregnated or silver catheters per local policy.
Subcutaneous tunnelling device (shunt passer) of adequate length.
Perforator or burr, bipolar diathermy, fine dural instruments.
Neuronavigation or ultrasound for small or distorted ventricles.
Laparoscopic set if the peritoneal catheter is to be placed laparoscopically.
Manometer and sterile pots for CSF samples.
anatomy: Kocher point (frontal entry) lies anterior to the coronal suture in the mid-pupillary line; the catheter is aimed towards the ipsilateral medial canthus in the coronal plane and the external auditory meatus in the sagittal plane, to reach the frontal horn anterior to the foramen of Monro.

The parieto-occipital entry (Frazier or Keen point) reaches the occipital horn and trigone; the catheter should pass along the long axis of the ventricle so that its tip lies in the frontal horn, away from the choroid plexus.
The choroid plexus lies in the body, trigone and temporal horn of the lateral ventricle but not the frontal horn: tips embedded in choroid block.

The tunnel crosses the neck superficial to the platysma, over the clavicle and down the anterior chest wall in the subcutaneous fat. Deep passage risks the pleura, the great vessels and the external jugular vein.
The peritoneum lies deep to the posterior rectus sheath or the transversalis fascia; preperitoneal fat can be mistaken for omentum.
criticalSafety: Infection prevention is a bundle, not a single act: first on list, limited theatre traffic, prophylaxis timed to incision, minimal handling of the implant, glove change before touching the shunt, antibiotic-impregnated catheters per local policy.
Confirm free CSF flow from the ventricular catheter and free distal run-off before the peritoneal catheter is placed.
Confirm the distal catheter is truly intraperitoneal: preperitoneal placement is a common cause of early failure.
Keep the tunnel subcutaneous across the neck and chest.
structuresAtRisk: Frontal horn wall, caudate nucleus and thalamus from a misdirected catheter
Superior sagittal sinus at a frontal burr hole placed too medially
Pleura, subclavian vessels and external jugular vein during tunnelling
Bowel and bladder at peritoneal entry
commonErrors: Multiple ventricular passes in small ventricles without image guidance.
A catheter tip in the brain parenchyma, the contralateral ventricle or the choroid plexus.
Preperitoneal placement of the distal catheter.
Handling the implant with contaminated gloves or leaving it exposed on the trolley.
Valve or connector placed directly under the scalp incision, where wound breakdown exposes it.
complications: Shunt infection, usually within the first months, from skin organisms; it normally requires removal of the whole system and external drainage.
Proximal obstruction (choroid plexus, debris, brain), valve failure, distal obstruction, disconnection or fracture of the tubing.
Over-drainage: postural headaches, slit ventricles, subdural hygroma or haematoma, particularly in normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Intracerebral or intraventricular haemorrhage along the catheter tract; seizures.
Abdominal: bowel perforation, peritoneal pseudocyst, ascites, inguinal hernia, catheter migration.
postop: CT or a shunt series according to local practice, to document catheter position as a baseline for future comparisons.
Neurological observations with a written trigger. Headache, vomiting, drowsiness or a falling GCS means shunt failure until proven otherwise.
Record the valve type and setting in the note and give the patient a shunt card. Re-check the setting of a programmable valve after any MRI.
Mobilise as the valve type allows; after normal pressure hydrocephalus shunting, watch for over-drainage headache on standing.
Teach the family and the patient the symptoms of shunt blockage and infection, and how to get urgent review.

steps.emphasis: Consent covers lifelong shunt dependence and the likelihood of revision, not just the operation.
Confirm ventricle size, the side and entry point on the scan, CSF results if a drain is present, and the valve chosen.
State the valve type and setting aloud, and that this is a shunt case requiring the infection bundle.
Time the antibiotic to incision; shunt infection is the complication that this case is most often judged by.
Horseshoe or ring, head turned away, shoulder roll so the tunnel runs in a straight line from scalp to abdomen.
Mark Kocher point or the parieto-occipital entry, the scalp incision and the abdominal incision before draping.
Use when the ventricles are small or distorted; otherwise anatomical landmarks are standard.
One continuous field from scalp to abdomen, with adhesive or iodine-impregnated drapes so no skin is exposed along the tunnel.
Curved incision so the valve and burr hole do not lie under the suture line.
A small cruciate opening and coagulated pia, just large enough for the catheter, so CSF does not track out around it.
Close the abdominal wound in layers as well; the scalp and abdominal wounds both cover the implant.
Include headache, vomiting and conscious level as shunt-failure triggers, and record the valve setting.
Record catheter lengths, valve type and setting, and CSF samples sent.

step.vps.shunt-handling.title: Shunt handling and preparation of the implant
step.vps.shunt-handling.why: Most shunt infections come from the patient's own skin flora carried onto the implant during the operation. The implant should stay in its packaging until needed, and should be touched as little as possible and only by fresh gloves.
how: Keep the shunt components in their packaging until the moment they are needed.
Change outer gloves before handling the shunt; one person handles it and keeps it away from the skin edges.
Prime the valve and catheters with sterile saline per the manufacturer's instructions, and check the valve opens and that a programmable valve is set to the agreed pressure.
Cover exposed skin and the wound edges with swabs or the drape while the shunt is in the field.
pitfalls: Leaving the opened shunt on the trolley through the cranial exposure.
Priming against the direction of flow and damaging the valve mechanism.

step.vps.abdominal-access.title: Peritoneal access
step.vps.abdominal-access.why: Entering the peritoneal cavity cleanly is what makes the distal catheter work. Preperitoneal placement is a common cause of early shunt failure, and blind entry can injure bowel, particularly after previous abdominal surgery.
how: Make a small incision, usually paraumbilical or subcostal, or use a laparoscopic port when there are adhesions, obesity or a previous failed distal catheter.
Divide the anterior rectus sheath, split the rectus muscle, and identify the posterior sheath and peritoneum separately.
Pick up the peritoneum between two clips, open it under direct vision, and confirm the cavity by seeing omentum or bowel serosa, not fat.
Place a purse-string suture on the peritoneum ready to secure the catheter.
pitfalls: Trocar entry without vision in an abdomen with previous surgery.

step.vps.tunnel.title: Subcutaneous tunnelling
step.vps.tunnel.why: The tunnel connects the cranial and abdominal wounds through a path the catheter will occupy for life. It must stay subcutaneous: too deep and it can enter the pleura or a vessel in the neck; too shallow and it erodes through the skin.
how: Pass the tunneller from the cranial wound to the abdominal wound (or the reverse), staying in the subcutaneous fat, with the free hand palpating the tip.
Make an intermediate incision behind the ear or in the neck if the tunneller is not long enough, rather than forcing it.
Cross over the clavicle superficially and keep the tip in view under the skin of the chest.
Pull the distal catheter through and protect both ends from contact with the skin.
structuresAtRisk: External jugular vein and subclavian vessels
Overlying skin in thin patients or infants
pitfalls: Diving under the clavicle and puncturing the pleura.
Tunnelling in a plane so superficial that the catheter later erodes.

step.vps.ventricular-catheter.title: Ventricular catheter insertion
step.vps.ventricular-catheter.why: The position of the ventricular catheter tip decides how long the shunt works. A tip in the frontal horn, free of the choroid plexus and the ventricular wall, has the best chance of staying open, and a single clean pass reduces the risk of haemorrhage.
how: Coagulate the pia and make a small corticotomy.
Pass the catheter with its stylet along the planned trajectory (or the navigation trajectory) to the depth measured on the scan, feeling for the loss of resistance as the ventricle is entered.
Remove the stylet and confirm free CSF flow; measure the opening pressure if needed and send CSF for cell count, protein and culture.
Advance the catheter off the stylet to the planned final length, and record the length at the outer table.
If there is no CSF after a pass, withdraw fully, re-check the landmarks or navigation, and limit the number of passes. Do not redirect inside the brain.
structuresAtRisk: Caudate nucleus, internal capsule and thalamus
pitfalls: Redirecting the catheter within the brain rather than withdrawing it fully.
Advancing too far, into the contralateral ventricle or the third ventricle.
Repeated blind passes in slit ventricles.

step.vps.connect-flow.title: Connecting the valve and confirming flow
step.vps.connect-flow.why: A disconnection or a valve that does not run is cheaper to find now than after the drapes come down. Spontaneous distal flow is the simplest test that the whole system works.
how: Bend the ventricular catheter at a right angle with a right-angle guide if used, and connect it to the valve in the correct direction of flow.
Secure every connection with a non-absorbable ligature, without cutting into the tubing, and anchor the valve to the pericranium.
Watch for spontaneous drip of CSF from the distal end of the peritoneal catheter, held below the head.
If there is no flow, check each part in turn: the ventricular catheter, the valve setting and orientation, and kinks in the tunnel.
pitfalls: Tying a ligature so tight that it cuts the catheter.

step.vps.peritoneal-placement.title: Placing the peritoneal catheter and closing the abdomen
step.vps.peritoneal-placement.why: The distal catheter needs enough length to allow growth or movement and a free intraperitoneal position. A catheter tightly secured in a narrow tract can be pulled out by movement; one left preperitoneal becomes a pseudocyst.
how: Insert the catheter freely into the peritoneal cavity with ample length, unless a short length has been agreed (for example in an adult with a large abdomen and no growth to allow for).
Confirm it passes without resistance and lies in the cavity; laparoscopic placement allows it to be seen directly.
Tie the purse-string around the catheter without occluding it, then close the posterior and anterior sheaths in layers.
Confirm CSF still drips from the catheter or that the valve pumps before the final layer is closed, where the valve design allows.
structuresAtRisk: The catheter itself (occlusion by the purse-string)
pitfalls: Occluding the catheter with the purse-string or the sheath closure.

step.vps.bailout.title: Bailout: when the shunt cannot be completed safely
step.vps.bailout.why: Some situations make a shunt unsafe to finish: cloudy or bloody CSF, a peritoneum that cannot be entered, or a ventricle that cannot be cannulated. Completing a shunt in these conditions usually guarantees early failure or infection.
how: Cloudy CSF or unexpected infection: send CSF, do not implant, and convert to an external ventricular drain.
Heavily bloodstained CSF or very high protein: consider an external drain or a reservoir until the CSF clears.
Peritoneum hostile or not enterable: close, and choose another distal site (ventriculo-atrial or ventriculo-pleural) as a planned procedure, or call a general surgeon for laparoscopy.
Ventricle not cannulated after a limited number of passes: stop, use navigation or ultrasound, and scan if there is any concern about haemorrhage.
Record the reason in the note and tell the family that a further procedure is planned.
pitfalls: Implanting a shunt into infected CSF to avoid a second operation.
